call.title: Story — The Lantern on Fen Lane
call.content:
Story — The Lantern on Fen Lane

## The story
The Lantern on Fen Lane. Mira was nine, and she had never once been allowed to light the lantern at the end of Fen Lane. Grandad Tobin did it every evening, humming the way he hummed when he was worried, though he said he never was. Tonight his knees were stiff with the cold, so he held out the long brass match-holder and said, "Go on, then." Mira's hands shook. The wick caught on the second try, and the glass turned gold. Down the lane, one window lit, then another, as if the houses had been waiting for her. "Who is it for?" she asked. "Anyone coming home late," said Grandad Tobin, "so they know the way." They walked back slowly, the light behind them, and Mira fell asleep still smelling the match.

## Names and facts

- Grandad Tobin — keeps the lantern; hums when he is worried

call.title: Story — The Lantern, Alone
call.content:
Story — The Lantern, Alone

## The story
The Lantern, Alone. On the first frosty evening of the year, Grandad Tobin's cough kept him by the fire, so Mira, who was nine, took the brass match-holder down from its hook by herself. Fen Lane was very quiet. Her breath made small clouds, and the lantern creaked on its post as if it were asking whether she was sure. She was not, entirely. The first match went out. The second one held, and the glass filled with gold, and somewhere behind her a door opened and Mrs Abara called out, "Thank you, love!" When Mira came back in, Grandad Tobin was humming, the way he did when he was worried, and then he stopped, because he had seen the light through the window.

## Names and facts
- Mira — nine; lives on Fen Lane with Grandad Tobin
- Grandad Tobin — keeps the lantern; hums when he is worried
- Mrs Abara — a neighbour on Fen Lane (new)

call.title: Story — Bramble and the Station Clock
call.content:
Story — Bramble and the Station Clock

## The story
Bramble and the Station Clock. Bramble was a small brown bear with a large green coat, and he had come a very long way. He sat on his suitcase under the station clock, which said a quarter to nine, and he waited for someone to read his label. The label said: Please be kind to this bear. A girl called Wren read it twice. Then she took off her scarf and wrapped it round his ears, because the wind came in through the arches and bears from far away feel the cold. "Where are you going?" she asked. Bramble did not know. Wren thought about it. "Home," she decided, "with us," and the clock struck nine, as if it agreed.

## Names and facts
- Bramble — a small brown bear in a large green coat, from far away
- Wren — a girl who reads his label

## Length
About 120 words (asked: 130).
